chapter_theme: Poverty as the worst suffering, one that has no comparison. It strips lineage, speech, learning and even a mother's regard, it returns day after day, and the chapter's last verse asks whether such a person should go on as they are.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the cruelty of poverty (1041-1045), its effects on the poor (1046-1049, including the speech of one poor man in 1048-1049), and what to do when it comes (1050).

1041.reading: If asked what is more painful than poverty, what's more painful than poverty is poverty.
1041.nuance: The sentence tries to find a comparison and fails. As Parimelazhagar says, if it has no equal, nothing can exceed it. Tautology is the argument.

1042.reading: The sinner called poverty comes, with this world and the next both lost.
1042.nuance: பாவி personifies it as an evil actor, although Manakkudavar reads a poor person who has the sin. The next world is lost, in his reason, because one can't afford charity, so poverty denies access to virtue itself. That cuts against the assumption that merit is equally open to all.

1043.reading: The desire called poverty destroys at once one's ancient descent and தோல்.
1043.nuance: The verse identifies poverty with desire, நசை. Parimelazhagar explains that where there's no craving there's no poverty, which is a remarkable reframing of an economic state as a mental one.

positions.position: தோல் means graceful speech, as Tolkappiyam uses it, and he rejects reading it as the body.
positions.quote: பழைய குடிவரவினையும் அதற்கு ஏற்ற சொல்லினையும் ஒருங்கே கெடுக்கும்.

positions.position: தோல் means fame, and the desire is a greed that poverty causes.

1044.reading: Even in the well-born, poverty brings the lapse from which degrading words are born.
1044.nuance: Parimelazhagar says what the words are: 'you must give to us'. He describes the lapse precisely: at the height of suffering, they forget their birth for a moment. The uncontrolled word is இளிவந்த, degrading, and that is the verdict of chapter 97 on such a person.

1045.reading: Within the suffering called poverty, many sufferings arrive and settle.
1045.nuance: Parimelazhagar lists a day's humiliations in order: going to the rich man's door, seeing him, being refused, accepting what he gives, and working out how to use it. One of the most vivid passages in his commentary, it is his own and not the verse's.

1046.reading: Even if they speak of good matters, fully understood, the words and meaning of the poor go slack.
1046.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a social mechanism and not a cognitive one: nobody listens, in case they come to feel obliged to help. So the meaning fails not in the speaker but in what the listeners are afraid of.

1047.reading: One in poverty unconnected with virtue is looked at as a stranger, even by the mother who bore him.
1047.nuance: The mother is again the limit case, as in 923. Parimelazhagar's reason is unsentimental: she fears that he would be taking and not giving.

positions.position: அறஞ்சாரா describes the poverty: it doesn't come from virtue nor yield virtue.
It describes the man, who has left the path of virtue because of poverty.

1048.reading: Will it come today too, the poverty that as good as killed me yesterday?
1048.nuance: The verse switches to first-person speech. Parimelazhagar imagines the speaker: someone who with great difficulty filled his belly yesterday. In போலும் he survived what felt like death, which means he will face it again.

1049.reading: One can even sleep in the middle of fire, but in the middle of poverty, there is no way of closing the eyes.
1049.nuance: Parimelazhagar explains the sleep in fire as a possibility through mantra and medicine, which rationalizes what looks like hyperbole. He hears the same speaker as in 1048.

1050.reading: If those without means don't fully renounce, they are death to salt and to gruel.
1050.nuance: The mockery falls on tiny things, salt and sour gruel: the poor person's mere continuing destroys these and nothing more.

positions.position: To renounce fully is to give up the body itself, for honour's sake; those left by kin have done everything else.
It is to give up attachment to wealth, which brings pleasure to the poor.
positions.quote: இது துறப்பாராயின், இன்ப முறலா மென்று கூறிற்று.

links.note: 423 says the mark of understanding is seeing the truth whoever says it. 1046 reports that a poor man's meaning falls flat however true it is. One gives the ideal, and the other the way the world listens.

959 says that speech reveals lineage as a sprout reveals soil. 1044 shows the signal failing: poverty brings degraded speech out of the well-born. Speech is a sign of poverty as well as lineage, so the test is less reliable than chapter 96 claims.

368 says there is no suffering for those without desire. 1043 makes poverty itself into desire, which Parimelazhagar glosses as: without craving there's no poverty. An ascetic insight enters the chapter on economic misery, while the rest of the chapter denies it.

378 says that the destitute would renounce if what they must suffer would pass. 1050, with the same துப்புரவு இல்லார், tells them to do it. The verse of fate explains why it doesn't happen, while this verse only mocks them for it.
247 keeps two forms of lack apart: no grace loses the next world, no wealth loses this one. 1042 collapses them: poverty takes both worlds. Grace alone turns out not to secure the next world.
'X என ஒரு பாவி' appears in both. Envy is the sinner in 168 and poverty in 1042, with both sending one down. Parimelazhagar links them himself. The state of being poor gets the same grammar as a vice.

The mother marks a moral limit twice. Her pain at drunkenness (923) still has love in it, because she's the most forgiving audience, and poverty does what drink couldn't by making her look at her son as a stranger.

source_issues: 1047: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and ends with இது பரிமேலழகருரை, stating that it is Parimelazhagar's commentary. It confirms that [#] entries across this block are not Manakkudavar's own and should not count as an independent voice.
1043: Parimelazhagar's lemma has தல்குரவு where the verse has நல்குரவு, apparently a transcription error.
1047: Pope's gloss has 'absolute poverty', dropping அறஞ்சாரா, though his couplet keeps it.
1050: Pope's gloss has 'renounce their bodies', from Parimelazhagar, and 'salt and water' for உப்பிற்கும் காடிக்கும், which also differs from his couplet's 'salt and vinegar'.
